title: Win-streak into level 9 with a flexible board

video.title: This Game Is a Set 18 Fast 9 (Flex) Masterclass...

player.name: Dishsoap
player.about: Two-time World Champion and co-curator of TFT Academy. The reference player for tempo and fast-9 lines: he decides the game plan from what the lobby gives him, not from a comp.

summary: A PBE game from the set's first week. Dishsoap takes Birthday Reunion and Spreading Roots, win-streaks through the early stages and levels to 9 with a flexible board built from whatever the shop offers rather than a preset comp.
thesis: Fast 9 is not a comp, it is an econ line that a strong early board pays for. This game shows the whole chain: a board that wins stage 2 and 3 pays streak gold on top of interest, augments that reward levels (Birthday Reunion pays a 2-star 5-cost at level 9) decide the timing, and the final board is chosen at 8 and 9 from the units that appear, held together by emblems rather than by a plan written before the game. Watch the levels and the gold, not the champions.

timeline.title: The augment is a commitment to a timeline
timeline.watch: Birthday Reunion pays out at levels 5, 7 and 9 (a 2-star 2-cost, a Thief's Gloves, a 2-star 5-cost). Note what he already has when he takes it and when in the game each reward lands relative to the standard level timings.
timeline.why: An augment that scales with level is a promise to reach those levels on time; taking it at 2-1 means the econ plan for the whole game is decided in round one.
timeline.question: Which of the three level rewards is the one that justifies the pick, and what does it demand of stages 3 and 4?

timeline.title: Strongest board every round, no exceptions
timeline.watch: Count how many rounds in stage 2 he fields a 2-star that arrived that same round, and how often the first components are combined on the units he has rather than held.
timeline.why: The win streak is the income line of a fast-9 game: streak gold plus interest plus zero HP lost. It is bought by fielding upgrades and slamming, not by saving.

timeline.title: Level 6 on schedule, no roll
timeline.watch: How much gold is on the bar after the level, and whether the shop is refreshed at all before 4-1. Also whether he keeps the 50-gold breakpoint through 3-5 while still streaking.
timeline.why: Fast 9 dies to a stage-3 roll. The level is the only purchase; the streak keeps the HP where it needs to be.
timeline.question: If the streak broke at 3-3, would you still be on the fast-9 line? What would have to be true?

timeline.title: Spreading Roots: emblems as flexibility
timeline.watch: Which units receive the two emblems and whether those emblems decide the line or keep two lines open. Notice how a random emblem changes which 4-costs are worth buying at 8.
timeline.why: An emblem is a free trait breakpoint; in a flex game it widens the set of boards that are strong, which is exactly what a player who has not committed wants.

timeline.title: Levels 7 and 8 before any rolldown
timeline.watch: Level 7 at 4-1 and 8 shortly after, and the size of the roll at 8: he buys the 4-costs that appear, not a shopping list. Track the gold left after the roll.
timeline.why: At 8 the 4-cost odds are three times what they are at 7; rolling before the level is paying triple. The stop condition is decided by the gold the level-9 plan needs, not by what the shop shows.

timeline.title: Items move to whoever the board became
timeline.watch: Items placed on early holders get moved to the 4-costs that actually arrived. Count how many items change hands between 4-1 and 5-1.
timeline.why: In a flex game the carry is decided by the shop; items that cannot move are a commitment made too early. Slam on holders whose items transfer.

timeline.title: Level 9 and the payout
timeline.watch: The round he hits 9, what the Birthday Reunion 5-cost turns out to be, and how the ninth slot is filled: a trait breakpoint, a second tank or a 5-cost carry.
timeline.why: Level 9 is only worth it if the board gets a slot that changes fights: a 5-cost that fits the items, or a breakpoint. Otherwise the gold was better spent two-starring the 4-costs.
timeline.question: Before he hits 9: which two units on his board would you two-star first with the gold instead? Was that the better line?

timeline.title: Positioning against the boards left
timeline.watch: How the layout changes between opponents in the last stages: where the carries stand against each remaining board and what gets moved after scouting.
timeline.why: With three or four boards left, every round is a known opponent; positioning is the last free strength in the game.

questions.q: Why is a win streak worth more than 50 gold in stage 2?
questions.a: Because it pays streak gold on top of interest and costs zero HP, and HP is what lets you reach level 9 while others stabilise. Interest alone caps at 5; a streak adds 2 to 3 more and protects the health that pays for the late levels.

questions.q: What makes this a flex game and not an Ashe game?
questions.a: The board is decided at 8 and 9 by the 4- and 5-costs that appear and the emblems he holds; items were slammed on holders that transfer. A player following a set comp would have rolled for specific units at 7 and lost the streak econ.

questions.q: Which single decision would break this line if done wrong?
questions.a: Rolling at stage 3. A stage-3 roll spends the interest and the level timing at once; the fast-9 econ never recovers and the augments that pay at 9 pay nothing.

sourceNote: Title, channel, date, length and the two named augments come from the video page. The stage guide is TFT Lab's reading of a fast-9 flex game and of what to watch for at each point; the video has no creator chapters, so stops are anchored to stages rather than timestamps.
